title: Cant Notes
cardBrief: Meilin learns the Bazaar's under-language by treating it like symptoms: repeated phrases, chalk marks, pauses that don't match the words.
keyTakeaways: **Listening for subtext**: Meilin starts hearing "the other language" under ordinary Bazaar chatter.
**Pattern logging**: She logs repeated phrases and chalk marks like symptoms, not like trophies.
**Recognition through context**: The meaning clicks when Oona uses small talk as warning and confirmation.
**Procedural response**: Meilin answers the signal with procedure; she bars a door and reduces exits.
**Documentation for recall**: She writes the translation down so it stays usable under stress.
**Ethical guardrails**: She keeps one ethics note attached: don't use the language to spend innocents.
content:
The Bazaar is loud in the way oceans are loud.

Not a single noise. An ecosystem of them.

Meilin learns quickly that if you listen only to the words, you miss the important part.

The important part is everything **around** the words.

The pause before a price. The way a vendor says “fresh” like a warning. The way a customer says “just looking” and still angles their body to block a line of sight.

And then there’s the other language.

The one people use when they want to be understood by exactly the wrong number of witnesses.

Meilin first hears it outside a stall that sells “map cases” and “scroll tubes” and other innocuous containers that always seem to be purchased by people with clean hands and dirty work.

Two men stand close enough to look like friends and far enough to look like strangers.

“Nice weather,” one of them says, smiling up at nothing.

The other nods. “Wind’s turning.”

Meilin keeps walking.

Her notebook stays in her satchel.

But her mind does what it always does: translates symptoms into causes.

If they were really talking about weather, no one would bother to stand like that. No one would check the alley behind them before they spoke. No one would smile with their mouth and not their eyes.

They aren’t talking about wind.

They’re talking about **risk**.

---

Meilin doesn’t learn Thieves’ Cant from a mentor who gives her a speech.

She learns it the way she learns everything that matters:

By watching it happen three times and refusing to pretend that’s coincidence.

The second time she hears it, it comes with a different surface story.

“Good stitching,” a woman says to a cloaked passerby, as if complimenting a hem.

The passerby doesn’t stop. “Needs reinforcement,” they reply, calm as cloth.

The woman’s hand drifts to the edge of a crate, fingers brushing a chalk mark shaped like a crescent.

Meilin notices because she always notices chalk.

Chalk is procedure. Chalk is someone trying to make the invisible visible.

She waits until the woman leaves, then steps in close and looks at the mark.

A crescent.

Beneath it, a tiny dot.

Not decoration.

A note.

Meilin doesn’t know what it means yet.

So she does the only honest thing:

She writes it down.

Not in big letters. Not in a way that would make her feel clever.

Just a small entry, tabbed and indexed like a patient chart:

Crescent + dot (crate corner). Heard: "Good stitching." Reply: "Needs reinforcement."

---

The third time, the meaning arrives without permission.

It happens at the back of a gear stall where Meilin sometimes does quiet work. A runner comes in with a basket and a face that looks too calm for the pace of their breathing.

Oona Marlow says, lightly, “You’re early.”

The runner answers, “Couldn’t sleep.”

Meilin catches it: Oona’s fingers tighten on the counter in the space between words. The runner’s eyes flick to the door, then to the alley beyond it.

Not insomnia.

Pressure.

Oona nods once and says, “Have you eaten?”

The runner’s voice stays even. “Not since yesterday.”

Meilin’s stomach goes cold.

She’s heard dockhands say “I haven’t eaten” to mean hunger.

This doesn’t sound like hunger.

This sounds like **I haven’t been safe**.

Oona slides a small paper packet across the counter (something that looks like a cheap snack). Her hand lingers on it half a beat too long.

The runner takes it without looking down.

Then Oona says, pleasantly, to no one in particular: “Weather’s turning.”

The runner replies, equally pleasant: “Wind’s turning.”

Meilin feels the click in her head.

Same phrase as the first time.

Oona glances toward the alley and, without changing expression, shifts a crate a finger’s width to expose a chalk crescent and dot.

Then she looks at Meilin, just once.

Not asking.

Measuring.

Meilin doesn’t speak.

She simply moves to the back door and bars it with a length of wood.

No drama. No questions. Just procedure.

If this is what she thinks it is, the best way to “answer” is to reduce exits.

Footsteps come a minute later: two sets, then three. Voices outside, casual and too close. Someone knocks in the polite way people knock when they want you to open the door so they can claim you let them in.

Meilin stays still and listens.

Oona murmurs, barely audible, “Hold steady.”

Meilin keeps her hands off her crossbow.

Not because she’s unarmed.

Because she understands, suddenly, that this language isn’t about bravery.

It’s about **coordination**.

About telling the right people the right thing while sounding like you’re talking about soup.

The footsteps drift away.

The pressure moves on to a softer target.

Oona exhales.

Meilin writes another line in her notebook:

**Weather’s turning / Wind’s turning = warning + confirmation.**

Then, after a beat, because she is Meilin and ethics are a kind of spine:

**Do not use on innocents. Do not sell names.**

---

Later, when someone tests her, and a stranger asks too casually where she sleeps and who she works for, Meilin answers in the Bazaar’s dialect without giving them anything real.

“Busy season,” she says mildly.

And when the stranger presses, smiling, Meilin adds, “Wind’s turning.”

The stranger’s smile tightens.

Not because they understand the *words*.

Because they understand what the words mean:

**I am not alone. I am not lost. Choose another mark.**

Meilin doesn’t enjoy that.

She doesn’t collect it like a trophy.

She treats it like every other tool in her kit:

Useful. Dangerous. Logged.
